prompt: What does the sampling distribution of the mean describe?

choices.text: The values inside one sample
choices.why: That is the distribution of one sample's data.

choices.text: Every value in the population
choices.why: That is the population's distribution.

choices.text: The means of every possible sample of a given size
choices.why: Right. It is the distribution of a statistic, the bridge between one sample and the population.

choices.text: How the sample was chosen
choices.why: That is the sampling method, from lesson 10.

prompt: The simulations in this lesson drew 2,000 samples from Horta's baskets. Why can a real study not do the same?
hint: What did the simulation have that a real study lacks?

choices.text: Computers are too slow for 2,000 samples
choices.why: Speed is not the problem; the population is.

choices.text: It has one sample, not the population
choices.why: Right. The simulation worked because the 400 baskets were treated as a known population.

choices.text: Drawing with replacement is not allowed in real surveys
choices.why: Replacement is a detail; the missing population is the obstacle.

choices.text: Sampling distributions only exist for simulations
choices.why: They exist for every statistic; a real study just cannot observe one directly.

prompt: According to the central limit theorem, what shape does the distribution of sample means approach as samples grow?

choices.text: The shape of the population
choices.why: That is what the data in a large sample looks like, not the means of many samples.

choices.text: Uniform
choices.why: The means pile up in the middle; they are not flat.

choices.text: Normal
choices.why: Right, whatever the population looks like, given independence and a finite standard deviation.

choices.text: Right-skewed
choices.why: Skew fades as samples grow; the means become symmetric.

prompt: A population has σ = 60. What is the standard deviation of the means of random samples of 36?
Write the standard deviation of the sample mean for samples of size n from a population with standard deviation s.
hint: The spread of the data, divided by the square root of the sample size.

prompt: Which condition does the central limit theorem need?
hint: What lets the many small pushes cancel?

choices.text: A normally distributed population
choices.why: That is precisely what it does not need: the population can have any shape.

choices.text: A sample of at least half the population
choices.why: Samples are usually a tiny fraction of the population.

choices.text: Independent draws, finite spread
choices.why: Right. Independence lets the pushes cancel; a finite standard deviation keeps σ ÷ √n meaningful.

choices.text: A symmetric sample histogram
choices.why: The sample can be as skewed as the population; it is the means that become symmetric.

prompt: As the sample size grew from 1 to 100, what happened to the centre of the 2,000 sample means?
hint: Look at the 'mean of the 2,000 means' column.

choices.text: It stayed put, near R$ 82.78
choices.why: Right. The sample mean is unbiased at every size; only the spread and the shape changed.

choices.text: It moved left towards the median, R$ 66.74
choices.why: The means centre on the mean, not the median, at every size.

choices.text: It moved right, pulled by the tail
choices.why: The tail is already included in the population mean; the centre does not drift.

choices.text: It became zero once standardised
choices.why: Nothing was standardised; the means are in reais.

prompt: Means of samples of 5 baskets had a skewness of 1.05, and of 30 baskets 0.34. What does that show about 'large enough'?
hint: Compare the skewness at each size.

choices.text: Five is enough for any population
choices.why: With a skewness of 1.05 the means of five are still clearly lopsided.

choices.text: The theorem fails for skewed data
choices.why: It works, just more slowly: by 100 the skewness was 0.12.

choices.text: Samples of 30 give exactly normal means
choices.why: 0.34 is close to symmetric, not exactly so.

choices.text: Skewed data needs larger samples first
choices.why: Right. How large is large enough depends on how skewed or heavy-tailed the population is.

prompt: Order these sample sizes by how closely the distribution of their means resembles a normal curve, from least to most.
hint: The bell sharpens as the samples grow.

prompt: Means of samples of 25 have a standard deviation of 12. What will it be for samples of 100?
A survey of 400 people has a margin that is too wide. Halving it with the same method needs how many people?
hint: Which number has a square root of 2?

choices.why: Doubling the sample divides the spread by √2, about 1.41, not by 2.
Fifty percent more people shrinks the spread by only about a fifth.
Right. The spread falls with √n, so halving it takes four times the sample.
Ten times the sample would shrink the spread by √10, about 3.2.

prompt: With σ = R$ 58.82, what is σ ÷ √n for samples of 400 baskets? Give two decimal places.
Horta collects 4,000 baskets instead of 400. What happens to the shape of their histogram?

choices.text: It becomes a normal bell, by the central limit theorem
choices.why: The theorem is about means of samples, not the values in one sample.

choices.text: It stays right-skewed, like the population
choices.why: Right. A larger sample looks more like the population, and the population is skewed.

choices.text: It becomes symmetric but stays wide
choices.why: Nothing in a larger sample removes the tail.

choices.text: It becomes left-skewed
choices.why: There is no reason for the tail to switch sides.

prompt: A convenience sample of the 60 nearest deliveries gives a very stable mean of 31.28 minutes, against a true 38.65. What does the theorem say about this?
hint: Does the theorem know how the sample was chosen?

choices.text: That the sample mean must be close to the truth
choices.why: Only for random samples; it has nothing to say about a biased one.

choices.text: That 60 is too small for the theorem to apply
choices.why: Size is not the problem; any number of near deliveries gives the same wrong centre.

choices.text: Nothing: it describes the wobble, not the bias
choices.why: Right. Bias is outside the theorem's reach; it assumes random, independent draws from the right population.

choices.text: That the true mean is probably 31.28
choices.why: The true mean across all neighbourhoods is 38.65; the sample was aimed at the wrong target.

prompt: Why is a proportion, such as the share of late deliveries in a sample, covered by the central limit theorem?
hint: Lesson 1: the mean of a yes/no column.

choices.text: Proportions are always normally distributed
choices.why: A proportion from a small sample is far from normal; it becomes approximately normal as the sample grows.

choices.text: It is a mean of zeros and ones
choices.why: Right. Lesson 1's trick: code late as 1 and on time as 0, and the share late is a sample mean.

choices.text: The theorem covers every statistic equally
choices.why: It is about means; a median, for example, has its own spread, not σ ÷ √n.

choices.text: Late deliveries follow a normal distribution
choices.why: Each delivery is late or not; the individual values are zeros and ones, nothing like a bell.

prompt: The distribution of a statistic over all possible samples of a given size is called its ___ distribution.
A colleague says: 'Our 5,000 order values are normally distributed, thanks to the central limit theorem, so the normal table gives the share above R$ 300.' What is wrong?
hint: Means of samples, or the values themselves?

choices.text: Nothing; 5,000 is far more than 30
choices.why: The count of values does not change their shape; it is the means of samples that become normal.

choices.text: The table should use n − 1
choices.why: The divisor is not the issue; the assumed shape is.

choices.text: It is about means, not single orders
choices.why: Right. Individual order values keep the population's skew, and the normal table will misjudge the tail.

choices.text: The theorem only applies to samples of exactly 30
choices.why: There is nothing special about exactly 30.
